abstract: Balancing selection encompasses a diverse set of evolutionary mechanisms that maintain genetic polymorphism within populations. However, both detecting balancing selection and distinguishing among its underlying mechanisms remain challenging. Recent advances in the generation of temporal genetic data and the application of machine learning offer new opportunities to address these challenges. In this study, we tested whether temporal genetic data improve the detection of balancing selection and the discrimination between two major balancing selection mechanisms, overdominance and negative frequency-dependent selection. Using forward simulations, we summarized temporal genetic data with features derived from a diverse set of population genetic summary statistics and trained support vector machine and random forest classifiers. Temporal data substantially improved the discrimination of balancing selection from neutral evolution, particularly when summarized by the first four moments of each statistic across time, increasing accuracy by up to 10%. Among individual summary statistics, simple measures of genetic diversity unexpectedly outperformed several more sophisticated statistics. In contrast, summary statistic-based approaches remained insufficient for effectively distinguishing overdominance from negative frequency-dependent selection, even when temporal information was incorporated. These results demonstrate the value of temporal genetic data for detecting balancing selection while highlighting the limitations of summary statistic-based inference for resolving alternative balancing selection mechanisms.
